William Chapman (born c. 2001 – died October 10, 2026) was a British former child television star and professional actor who gained prominent media attention in the late 2000s. Born and raised in Buckinghamshire, England, Chapman showed early performance talent and went on to secure highly visible roles on major networks like the BBC and ITV.
At the time of his tragic death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in South Yorkshire, Chapman was 24 years old. Following the incident, substantial public debate erupted regarding his health, actions, and background, prompting clarification from authorities and media reports regarding his childhood fame and adult personal struggles.

Early Life and Childhood Acting Career
Chapman grew up in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire. Recognizing his early dramatic potential, his family enrolled him in the prestigious Jackie Palmer Stage School. The agency is highly regarded in the United Kingdom for developing young British performers and securing mainstream industry opportunities.
Through the agency, Chapman transitioned rapidly from a student performer to a working child actor, landing professional credits listed across national databases and IMDb:

•May Contain Nuts (2009, ITV): His most substantial breakout role occurred in this two-part, prime-time satirical comedy-drama adapted from the John O'Farrell novel. Credited directly as Alfie Chaplin, a nine-year-old Chapman performed as a main ensemble cast member alongside renowned British mainstays, including BAFTA-nominated actor Darren Boyd and Shirley Henderson (widely recognized as Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter series).

•True Stories (BBC): Chapman was cast as the lead character in an episode of the historical docudrama television series True Stories. He portrayed a young Edward Jenner, the pioneering 18th-century English physician and scientist famously credited with developing the world’s first smallpox vaccine.

•Pan (2015, Warner Bros.): As an adolescent, Chapman branched into major Hollywood cinema. He secured a background acting role on the set of the live-action Peter Pan prequel fantasy film directed by Joe Wright, which starred high-profile actors Hugh Jackman, Rooney Mara, and Amanda Seyfried.

Explicitly Debunking Medical Claims: No Autism, Learning Disabilities, or Deafness
In the immediate, chaotic aftermath of the zoo enclosure breach, widespread misinformation flooded social media platforms like X and TikTok. Commentators and online advocates speculated that his dangerous proximity to an apex predator was driven by physical or developmental disabilities.

However, public records, professional colleagues, and official statements have definitively confirmed that William Chapman did not suffer from autism, a learning disability, or hearing loss.

1. He Was Not Deaf
Early eyewitness accounts described Chapman pacing erratically by the enclosure while remaining completely unresponsive to the screams of nearby families. This led to a viral theory that he was deaf and could not hear the warnings.
The investigation confirmed that Chapman possessed normal hearing but was actively wearing headphones. He consciously tuned out the frantic vocal alerts of onlookers as he moved down from the elevated platform toward the perimeter.

2. No Autism Spectrum Disorder or Cognitive Impairments
Journalistic evaluations and community announcements directly debunked theories asserting that Chapman had a severe learning disability or lacked the neurological capacity to understand basic danger.

quoted_text:
Today we're standing up XBOX LABS (https://t.co/dJSufI1vni). Here is the note that I sent to the team:

Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we've helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.
To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here.  Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We've spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren't changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology that is game design led without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

quoted_text:
Ok, well I'm going to talk about a token that everyone knows but has been very much forgotten about, and I thought I would never ever write about.

The bull case for BAT (please stay with me): 

Brave is one of the few crypto native companies that won in the real world. $100M+ annualized revenue. 126M monthly users, 55M Daus. Its own search index doing 2.5B queries a month. 

People use it because it is fast and private performant browser, not because of a token anymore (although they did use the token to incentivise growth for a long time).

Its advertising business is very successful, alongside its paid search API. 

BAT trades at a $170M market cap. Fully circulating. No unlocks.

That is 1.7x revenue on a business growing users around 25% a year (not completely verified). And the $100M figure is from early 2025, 40M users ago. I can't find a more up to date figure. 

The token never captured any of that. That is why it went nowhere for five years. Roadmap 4.0 is the first real attempt to fix it.

TLDR on 4.0:

Unified Brave Wallet - Cards, self-custody crypto and Rewards in one interface, native in the browser.

BravePay - A private, self-custody stablecoin payments layer. 

Brave Rewards Card - Virtual and physical. Earn BAT on everyday spend. They already have 150k on the waitlist before launch.

Buybacks (Big change) - A share of net revenue from the wallet, card and BravePay buys BAT. Opportunistic buybacks on top, disclosed publicly.

Distribution is Brave's massive edge, as it is for all successful businesses. 

Every crypto neobank is fighting for its first million users. Brave starts with 55M people opening the product every day. The wallet is already installed. Acquisition cost is zero.

BAT printed an all-time low in August. It has doubled since and still sits 94% below its 2021 high. The rerate has barely got going. 

Every token has a bear case, so in this case Brave has equity. Token holders technically don't own the $100M. Buybacks come from the new product lines only, and the percentage is undisclosed.

Bought BAT is not burned. It funds user rewards, and some recipients will sell.

The card has no launch date yet I don't think.

So this rerating that I think is possible is not a claim on Brave’s revenue. It is a cheap option on Brave monetising 126M users through payments, with BAT as the reward and the buyback sink. At 1.7x revenue with a new structural bidder, I think that option is mispriced.

What is it worth? I don't know. The buyback percentage isn’t disclosed and the new products aren’t live.

BAT traded at a $420M market cap last December. Before Roadmap 4.0, before buybacks and 20M users ago. Getting back there is 2.4x.

Every $10M a year of buybacks is roughly 6% of today’s market cap. Brave does $100M+ in revenue before payments even launch.

I’m not underwriting a specific number. I’m underwriting that I think $170M is the wrong one. If I'm wrong and nothing happens then I think the risk is underperformance more than anything. 

The thing that I think is also interesting here is a bigger pattern: 

Old tokens attached to businesses that survived are reworking value capture. Brave is unique as it has an unrivalled sizeable user base it can monetise and finally return value to token holders. 

Also, fun fact is Brave's founder invented javascript and co founded Mozilla.  

DYOR, NFA.

One life, it's worth a shot etc.

The upgrade will replace the existing TowerBFT consensus mechanism with Votor, aiming to reduce transaction finality from approximately 12.8 seconds to 150 milliseconds. text:
Some Democrats are saying that I did not run any analyses on the Amacher audio. Other Democrats are saying that I am stupid because "analysis" is not spelled "analyses". These are the raw results. The menu check remains. Everything is easily reproducible from the text below.

# Was the Lindner call "made with ElevenLabs v4 Turbo"? Interim analysis

*Status: interim, 2026-10-13. Three of five planned tests are complete and independently audited. The phone-menu match (V1) and the request for the publisher's original file (V4) are still open. Spec: `~/talarico/VOICE_AGENT_TEST_SPEC.md`. Every number below comes from saved run outputs and audits under `/mnt/lanes/projects/talarico/runs/`, with verified second copies under `/staging/talarico_evidence_copy/voice/`.*

## The claim
A reply to the call recording said it was "made with elevenlabs v4 turbo which you can use to make live voicecalls about any topic you want." On this theory, the "staffer" who answered was a live AI voice agent, not a person.

The claim is technically possible:
- ElevenLabs released **Eleven v4 and v4 Turbo on 2026-09-28**, about two weeks before the call. Turbo is built for real-time voice agents. ElevenLabs reports about 150 ms to first speech and voice cloning from about 10 seconds of audio.
- ElevenLabs' own documentation, saved by the V2 lane, confirms that `eleven_v4_turbo` can run Agents. It also shows agents can **add continuous background sound** (office, typing, hold music) and connect to the phone network through Twilio or SIP.

## Why the earlier "not AI" analysis does not settle this
The first analysis found a real two-party phone recording:
- the staffer side is cut off at phone bandwidth (about 4 kHz);
- the caller side is wideband;
- the line noise is continuous.

That rules out a file assembled after the fact. **A live AI agent answering a phone call would produce exactly the same pattern.** The "90–95% not AI" figure from the first analysis has been withdrawn. So the question needed new tests.

## Bottom line so far
**The audio neither supports nor rules out the ElevenLabs claim.** None of the three completed tests can tell the staffer apart from a real v4 Turbo agent, and none points toward an agent either.
- ElevenLabs' own detector cannot recognize v4 Turbo at all.
- A live v4 Turbo agent, measured with the same tools, shows turn-taking within the staffer's range.

The test most likely to settle the question is the phone-menu match (V1), which is still open.

## What was done

### 1. Measuring the real call (V0, independently audited by A-V0)
- A measurement tool was built and checked on synthetic audio with known answers ("V0 selftest PASS").
- It was run on all four releases: the 6:40 full call, the 2:26 first call, and the 55 s and 47 s clips.
- An independent auditor then checked each of its 50 candidate events by eye on a spectrogram. **4 were confirmed, 36 rejected and 10 unclear.**

What holds up:
- **Two times the staffer started talking before the caller finished:**
- full call, about 6:20: her "So he should be—" under his "And this is the Hope—";
- first call, about 2:02: her "Yeah, well if you send it…".
- **No confirmed backchannels from the staffer** (short "okay"/"mm-hm" while the caller talks).
- **No confirmed caller interruptions.**
- **No confirmed moments where one voice reacts to the other mid-overlap.** So the "two voices stitched together" claim (TrueMedia, via Newsweek) found nothing either way.
- **Background:** her pauses carry real non-steady activity on her end of the line, about 38 dB above the quiet floor in one pause, just before a stretch the publisher muted for "background audio privacy". Whether it is another person talking, or typing, is not confirmed.

### 2. A real ElevenLabs v4 Turbo agent as a control (V2, independently audited by A-V2)
- **The setup:** an agent on `eleven_v4_turbo` with a stock voice and a **fictional** facility ("Riverside Center"). No voice cloning, and no use of Lindner's name. It was told to ask for a code, "check" names, and put callers on hold, with office background sound on.
- **The runs:** the caller's actual turns, cut from the released recording, were played into the agent at their original timing in **5 accepted live runs**. Total cost **$0.90**: $0.22, $0.17, $0.17, $0.16, $0.15.
- **The failed attempt:** one further attempt failed on ElevenLabs' side ("LLM Cascade Error: TimeoutError"). It was excluded and replaced.
- **The measurement:** each agent output was compressed through a phone codec (G.711) and measured with the same tool.

The harness's own automatic comparison labeled the result "moderate against an AI agent". **That label was wrong and has been withdrawn.** It used V0's unvalidated counts instead of the audited ones, and it read the rule backwards: the agent started talking over the caller *more* often than the staffer did. The independent re-analysis replaced it.
| Measure | Real call (audited) | v4 Turbo agent (audited) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Starts before the caller finishes | 1 per call (2 calls) | 0–1 per run | No weight: the agent does this too |
| Gap from caller stop to reply | validated points −0.43 s and −0.40 s | demonstrated range −0.60 s to +2.49 s | No weight: inside the agent's range |
| Short "okay"s while the caller talks | none confirmed | none confirmed | No weight |
| How fast she stops when talked over | not comparable | — | Not assessable (the replayed caller cannot react) |
| The 3-minute hold | publisher replaced it with silence | — | Not assessable |
| Background sound | present in her pauses | agents can add it | Weak at most, as fixed in advance |
The auditor also compared levels after the phone codec:
- Agent greeting levels were about −20 to −19 dBFS, against about −23 dBFS for the real greeting.
- The agent's pauses were noisier (median about −61 dBFS against about −76 dBFS), because of its configured office ambience.
These differences come from settings and are not a fingerprint of synthesis.
### 3. ElevenLabs' own AI Speech Classifier (V3)
- **Real recordings:** every released recording scored **2% ("Very unlikely… ElevenLabs")**. That covers the 55 s clip, the first two minutes of the full call, and the staffer section of the first call.
- **Positive control:** audio from **our own v4 Turbo agent** also scored **2%**, both straight from the agent and after phone compression.
- **Negative control:** known human speech (Talarico, Sept 30, phone-compressed) scored 2% in one test and **39%** in another.
- **ElevenLabs' own FAQ, saved:** the classifier "does not reliably classify audio generated with the Eleven v3 model". It says nothing about v4.
**Conclusion: the classifier cannot detect v4 Turbo, so its 2% on the Lindner audio carries no weight either way.**
## Still open
- **V1, the phone-menu match.** Both released calls start with Lindner's phone menu ("If you are a hospital… press 1"). Kevin records the menu by calling the published number late at night, silently, hanging up before anyone answers. That recording is then aligned with the released menus:
- **Same recording:** the calls went through Lindner's real phone system. That is strong evidence against an agent on some other number.
- **Different wording at the same time of night:** moderate evidence the calls did not go through Lindner's system.
- **Same wording, different recording:** weak.
- **V4, the original file.** The unedited recording from Current Revolt or Rhein Amacher, including the 3-minute hold. Hold music or a hold message from Lindner's phone system would point to a real Lindner line. The request is drafted and has not been sent yet.
- **V5.** The final findings note, a fresh independent audit, and the final read.
## Limits
- The agent control is **one** model (v4 Turbo), **one** voice, **one** prompt and **one** set of turn-taking settings. It does not cover every possible agent configuration.
- The caller's turns were replayed, so they could not react to the agent. Interruption and yielding behavior therefore could not be compared.
- The released audio is edited: publisher mutes at 1:03–1:06 and 1:13–1:16, and the hold replaced with digital silence.
- Nothing here establishes who the staffer was, or whether what she said was true.
- **None of this bears on whether anyone was a patient anywhere.**
## Sources

- ElevenLabs v4 launch: [TechCrunch](https://t.co/B1AM8zNncd) · [TechTimes](https://t.co/zt4uS38a9k)
- ElevenLabs classifier: <https://t.co/HivZT4dcDw>. FAQ saved 2026-10-12 as V3I evidence.
- TrueMedia "stitching" comment: [Newsweek, 2026-10-12](https://t.co/rrgghiiMjs)

- Run folders:

- `V0-codex` and `A-V0-codex` (measurement and its audit);
- `V2prep-codex` (agent harness, `control_runs/1..5`);
- `A-V2-codex` (`comparison_corrected.json`, AUDIT.md);
- `V3-interactive` (classifier runs and screenshots).

text:
SpaceX 今天收在156.54美元，跌了4.2%。评论区第一反应是解禁砸盘? 马斯克唱空内存被制裁了？同一天，印度那边又出了个坏消息：执政党背后的组织公开要求政府别给 Starlink 发牌照。 $SPCX  一个是远期利好，一个是眼下的麻烦，都还没有结论。

先说股价。全天成交6700万股左右，纳斯达克给的日均量是9900万股，今天大概只有平时的三分之二。不过这个平均数被8月刚上市那阵的天量撑高了，换成中位数，平常一天八千万股出头，今天也就少了两成。所以我只敢说：没看到有人集中出逃，但也谈不上“没人卖”。10月9日那批3.28亿股解禁当天，成交也只有9200万股，没有放量。今天芯片股、韩国股市都在跌，SpaceX 跟着大盘走的可能更大。具体为什么跌，没人有完美答案，这只是我的推测。

再说 FAA。X 上有人喊“FAA 批了一年456次”，其实只是开始审。现在星舰基地一年最多飞25次，SpaceX 申请分两步：先提到一年100次，过几年再到456次，差不多每个工作日两次。公众意见收到11月30日，业内估计这种完整环评要一年半到两年。这事为什么要紧？手机直连卫星要靠天上卫星够密，新一代 V3 卫星得靠星舰去运，星舰能飞多勤，先卡在这份审批上。

然后是印度。出来喊话的叫 SJM，是 RSS 管经济的分支，RSS 是莫迪所在人民党的思想母体。它说 Starlink 卫星之间用激光传数据，流量可能绕开印度的网关，政府想断网、想监控都难，还把美国关税扯进来：你能拿国家安全加关税，我也能拿国家安全封 Starlink。SJM 不是监管部门，政府听不听还不知道，也没证据说今天的跌和它有关。

所以 Starlink 这条线现在两头卡：天上，卫星能发多快要看 FAA；地上，最大的新市场之一要看印度通信部。眼前最近的日子是10月26日，下一批3.28亿股可以卖了。

你手里有 SpaceX 吗？解禁、FAA、印度这一出，你是拿着、加仓，还是先跑？评论区聊聊。

text:
Google Play 开放“个人 App”：用 AI Studio 手搓的安卓应用，不用注册开发者也能直接装进自己手机

10 月 13 日，Google 宣布了一项对普通玩家非常友好的更新：你在 Google AI Studio 里让 AI 写出来的安卓 App，现在可以直接通过 Google Play 安装到自己的手机上运行了。整个过程只需要一个普通的 Google 账号，根本不用去折腾开发者注册。同一天上线的，还有 Ask Play 的应用对比功能，以及帮玩家淘游戏的新工具 Game Finder。

【谁能先用上？】

“个人 App”功能从今天起逐步推送，首批覆盖“包括美国在内的部分市场”，且仅限 18 岁以上用户。不过 Google 官方只点名了美国，没透露具体还有哪些国家和地区。由于 Google Play 未在中國大陆提供服务，大陆用户暂时还无缘体验。

【怎么把 AI 写的 App 装进手机？】

以前在 AI Studio 里虽然也能做安卓 App，但想装到手机上，对于不懂开发的普通人来说简直是劝退现场：你得拿根数据线把手机连上电脑，还要进设置里一步步打开调试授权，门槛相当高。

现在整个链路彻底打通了。你只需要在 AI Studio 里像聊天一样提需求，让 AI 帮你生成安卓应用（也就是现在很火的 vibe coding，靠聊天驱动写代码），接着就能直接通过 Google Play 把它推送到自己的设备上。Google Play 副总裁 Sameer Samat 在推文里特意强调，这属于“无线安装”，彻底甩掉了数据线。据 Engadget 报道，安装好的应用会躺在你 Play 商店新增的“个人库”里；除了手机，只要能用 Play 商店的平板和电脑也都能装。

这些“手搓”出来的 App 仅限你自己的设备使用，不会进入 Play 商店的公开目录，别人也搜不到。Google 表示，未来几个月内会开放分享功能，让你能把做好的小工具发给“亲近的朋友和家人”，但目前还只能自己独享。

【要交 25 美元注册费吗？要审核吗？】

如果只是做给自己用，完全免费。要知道，注册一个正式的 Google Play 开发者账号得交 25 美元的一次性注册费，而“个人 App”直接帮你省下了这笔钱和繁琐的流程。

至于大家关心的审核问题，官方公告里只明确了一种情况：如果你哪天想把自己的 App 公开上架、让所有人都能下载，那就必须升级为正式的开发者账号；到那时，你的 App 也得和其他正规应用一样，老老实实走完信任、安全和质量审核流程。

那自用阶段到底审不审？官方正文里巧妙地避开了这个话题。不过据第三方媒体 AndroidPure 透露，在 Google 放出的界面示意图上，有一行小字写得很清楚：这类 App 只有创建者本人可见、可安装，不会经过 Google Play 的审核。

【安全问题怎么兜底？】

官方在公告里只丢下一句定心丸，说这些个人 App “私密、安全，且与公开商店相互隔离”。但具体到底怎么个安全法？安卓自带的恶意软件扫描工具 Play Protect 会不会扫它们？这些 AI 写出来的代码会怎么处理手机里的个人数据？对于这些核心细节，Google 这次守口如瓶，只字未提。

【同场加映：用 AI 挑应用、找游戏】

除了降低做 App 的门槛，Google 这次还顺手升级了找应用和找游戏的体验：

1. Ask Play 支持应用PK了

Ask Play 是内置在 Play 商店里的 AI 助手，以前你向它提问，它会给你推荐应用。从今天起，它学会了“拉表格做对比”——能直接把几款同类 App 放在一起，帮你梳理核心差异和真实的用户评价。不过官方同样没交代这个功能会在哪些地区开放。

2. 在 Gemini 里直接逛 Play 商店

全新的 Play in Gemini 功能会把 Play 商店里的应用、游戏和开发者内容直接接入 Gemini 的对话框里。官方承诺“很快”就会向所有 Gemini 用户推送，但还没给出确切的时间表。

3. 更懂你的找游戏神器 Game Finder

这是一个全新的游戏发现工具，底层的核心叫“Gamer DNA（玩家基因）”。它会根据你平时的游玩习惯和填过的偏好，为你生成专属画像；你也可以手动勾选喜欢的游戏、类型和玩法来随时微调。

当你点开一款新游戏时，它会非常直观地告诉你：和你口味相似的玩家玩得开不开心、你关注的人里有几个正在玩、大家的评价汇总，甚至还会告诉你最近哪些游戏正在火、为什么火。该功能今天起率先面向美国用户推出英文版，其他市场“即将跟进”。

4. 游戏社交与轻度竞赛

今天同步在所有市场推开的还有 Sprints，这是一种限时 48 小时的微型挑战赛，支持 2 到 5 人组队比拼。另外，所有游戏的详情页里都加上了“社区帖子”板块，玩家们可以在里面直接提问、交流攻略，覆盖所有游戏和语种，还自带实时自动翻译。

text:
1) Trying again.
 TLDR: Everyone can win. Open-source, frontier labs, infrastructure, applications and most importantly the American people.
 
I understand all of the jitters about Anthropic losing share, real rates, spreads and second derivatives. Still think the most likely future outcome is a hybrid, multi-model future where almost everyone wins, open-weight tokens are likely the overwhelming majority of tokens, the dominant frontier model companies still do well albeit perhaps not the outcome that seemed possible in May and AI infrastructure/applications benefit immensely from the increased fragmentation, competition and lower margins at the model layer.
 
Lower margins at the model layer mechanically drive higher compute demand as long as someone is willing to pay for the training. And Jensen is obviously willing to be the “trainer of last resort.” As below-market compute contracts signed in 24/25 roll-off and reprice higher, cloud and neocloud revenue should continue to accelerate which will help address financing fears; I think we may be near peak external financing for this buildout. Noteworthy that using data from 3Fourteen Research, B200 clusters will generate a 37% IRR *if* their rental price declines 40% per year. Prices are still going up, but that IRR math is too ridiculous to print. 37% IRRs available at scale should get funded.

Re: this weekends controversy about MOUs, Anthropic’s $413 billion of real contractual commitments sounds scary. Reality is that it works out to roughly $31 billion of annual cloud spend, which is easily internally financed given their reported ARR, and $161 billion of spend at Broadcom which will be financed by Broadcom and private credit.

Continue to believe fragmentation at the model layer is the best outcome for ordinary Americans and humans everywhere. As I have said before, do not trust any 5-20 individuals to make the best possible decisions about the direction of this technology. I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that they encompass the diversity of human values across the world and richness of human variation. And I want an AI that shares my own personal values. Safety, freedom and the maximization of human agency through democratization, distribution and diffusion vs. centralization. History has spoken on the dangers of the latter path.

Finally, from my perspective anything that slows this buildout down is net positive over the long-term as the biggest risk and worst outcome is an *actual* overbuild. We are structurally short watts, wafers and increasingly capital. That is all good. God forbid we were still in ZIRP, TSM ramped capex to 3x their current plan and we weren’t short turbine blades: there would almost certainly be an overbuild and a bubble. That would be terrible. Slower and smoother for longer is better both for investors and for the world. A terrible cyber event is the most plausible near term bear case IMHO, but AI cyberdefense ramping quickly and I was happy to hear Sholto say that cyber probably becomes defense dominant in the near future.

Prediction markets are becoming institutional. The infrastructure underneath them needs to catch up.

Today, Furnace is coming out of stealth.

We’ve raised $3.5M led by @NorthIslandVC, with participation from @vaneck_us, @recvcx, @hi_Reverie, and angels from The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), Public, and Commonweal Ventures.

We started Furnace around one question:

What does this contract actually represent?

As prediction markets expand across venues, the same economic exposure can be represented through contracts with different names, structures, rules, timing, and settlement mechanics. Some represent the same underlying exposure. Others look similar but are materially different.

Traditional financial markets rely on common identifiers and reference data to represent instruments and exposures consistently across trading, position, and risk systems. Prediction markets are developing without that common framework.

Furnace is building it.

We assign persistent canonical identities to economic exposures and map venue-specific instruments to them, while preserving the differences in rules, settlement, and other terms that can matter.

This gives institutions and builders a common foundation for integrating prediction markets into existing financial infrastructure and building new products around them.

Our goal is to create a common language for prediction-market exposures, making them consistently identifiable and usable across financial systems and products.

We’re grateful to our investors and partners who have helped us get here.
If you’re trading, building, or creating infrastructure around prediction markets, we’d love to talk → https://t.co/KE5vxCFs3c

The first AI Assistant Consumer Travel Report is live!

We spent the past week testing travel capabilities across 5 AI assistants: Instinct, Muse, GrokBot, Dots & Miso

🥈 Instinct - very fast but couldn't do rescheduling

Each assistant was tested across the following dimensions:
1. Booking time
2. Onboarding flow
3. Booking execution
4. Seat selection
5. Travel profile
6. Cancellation
7. Rebooking
8. Proactiveness

> Everyone biased towards cheaper options except Miso, who wasn't able to book basic economy flights

text:
Today we're standing up XBOX LABS (https://t.co/dJSufI1vni). Here is the note that I sent to the team:

Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we've helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.
To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here.  Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We've spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren't changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology that is game design led without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

text:
英国《金融时报》今天有一篇报道，讲中国 AI 公司算力不够用，干脆成批买英伟达的游戏显卡和工作站显卡来顶班。FT 的标题说，北京想让科技公司戒掉英伟达，但这条路走得很费劲。

看完的感觉是，国产芯片在使劲追，但缺口一时还填不上。

FT 引述多名业内人士的观点，中国科技公司今年已经买了 100 多万颗英伟达的游戏和工作站芯片。这些芯片本来不是为大型 AI 设计的，一类是打游戏用的显卡，一类是做设计、渲染的专业显卡。本来该在电脑里跑 3A 大作的卡，现在被拉进机房干 AI 的活，也算是转行了。（游戏玩家：😲）

国产芯片其实很努力。华为、阿里巴巴、百度、寒武纪这些公司带着，国产 AI 芯片今年产量翻了一倍多，境内供应预计能到 350 万颗，其中大约 100 万颗是在海外制造的。但整体需求估计远超 500 万颗。就算把英伟达这 100 多万颗加上，盘子还是不够大。

被拉来顶班的主要是 RTX Pro 6000D、RTX Pro 5000 和 RTX 5090，都符合美国出口管制的规定，可以合法卖到中国。和华为的旗舰芯片昇腾 910C 比，它们大多数运算都更慢。但简单的活是干得了的，比如预填阶段。预填说白了，就是模型先把用户的提问从头读一遍，还没开始一个字一个字往外蹦答案的那一步。主力干不过来，替补先把读题的活接了。

英伟达的回应话里有些不满。它说自 2022 年以来，中国本土的工作站芯片和显卡厂商增长得前所未有，而美国企业两头受限，一头是过时的美国出口管制，连近五年前推出的游戏产品都还管着，另一头是中国自己限制进口美国产品。两边都在拦，夹在中间的英伟达当然有话要说。

中国公司离不开英伟达，有一部分原因是 CUDA。CUDA 是英伟达的编程平台，开发者写 AI 程序基本都靠它。大多数中国科技公司在被迫转向华为的 CANN 之前，早就用惯了 CUDA，而 CANN 被认为不太好上手。用惯的工具是很难戒的，换平台就像换了键盘布局，手还是往老地方摸。DeepSeek 正在和华为合作改进软硬件，华为也在用 AI 工具加快把代码从 CUDA 搬到 CANN 上，让 AI 帮忙摆脱对英伟达的依赖，这个思路还挺妙。

下一款芯片已经有人排队了。两名直接了解计划的人士称，英伟达正在推出新的工作站芯片 RTX Pro 5500，性能比现在卖给中国的产品更强。中国公司表达的采购意愿加起来竟然超过 200 万颗，但这款芯片最快要到今年底才开始出货。

如果没有新的限制，RTX Pro 5500 可能让英伟达在中国的份额再往上走。美国实施出口管制之前，英伟达在中国 AI 芯片市场的份额曾经超过 90%。

监管这头也在看。一家中国大型科技公司的高管对 FT 说，监管机构正在和科技公司沟通，了解它们对 RTX Pro 5500 的需求是不是真有必要，"坦白说，答案会是有必要"。

出口管制挡住了最强的芯片，但挡不住需求。国产芯片翻了一倍还是不够，游戏显卡就成了现成的补丁。RTX Pro 5500 能不能顺利卖进来，要看华盛顿和北京两边的态度，这一回合还没有结果。

text:
都说美国东西贵到吃不起，摩根大通今天交的财报却是另一幅画面：这个季度，它的客户用借记卡和信用卡一共刷了5395亿美元，比去年同期多了一成。信用卡欠款也在涨，平均余额从去年同期的2344亿美元涨到2501亿。最反直觉的是，还不上钱的人反而少了，信用卡净坏账率从上个季度的3.34%降到2.91%。

这个“多刷了一成”: 里面有物价，同样一车菜、一箱油，今年就得多刷几块；也有客户变多，它的活跃手机银行用户一年多了7%。CFO 说油费、旅行这些类别都在涨。所以刷得多，不能直接读成大家日子更宽裕了。

坏账率下降也要看是谁的账。摩根大通是美国最大的发卡行之一，但它的客户不等于全美国，信用差、收入低的人群未必在它的账上。管理层给的全年坏账率指引仍在3.2%左右，一个季度好看，可能有季节因素。

我的理解是：至少在这家银行的客户身上，高利率和高物价还没把人压垮，大家一边抱怨一边继续刷。Dimon 在财报里也点了名：通胀、资产价格高、利率上升，这些力量也许可控，但他准备好应对各种结果。接下来要看的是，卡债余额继续涨的时候，坏账率能不能守在3%上下；两条线要是一起往上走，那才是消费者真撑不住了。  $JPM

I’m excited to share that I’ve joined @Morpho to lead all things commercial as Head of GTM.

@PaulFrambot and team are visionaries and world-class builders. It’s a privilege to team up with them.

Blog: https://t.co/aE8sU8L3QE

What’s Morpho?

Morpho is an open credit network that enables people and agents to build customizable onchain lending, borrowing, and yield products.

Morpho protocols, smart contracts, and blockchains are the infrastructure making it possible. Morpho is a pure technology layer, with composability and security at the center of its design.

The why

Morpho makes it dead simple for our partners - fintechs, brokerages, exchanges, and banks - to build revenue-generating products that help their users put their assets to work. In parallel, this helps unlock new distribution for lenders and asset issuers.

Historically, spinning up credit products meant building pricing, risk and liquidation systems from scratch, and spending months on integrations before the first loan went out.

Morpho collapses this into open infrastructure: liquidity, rates, and liquidations run onchain, in markets anyone can access.

We’re growing

More than $17B is now deposited on Morpho protocols, up 3.4x since the beginning of 2025.

So far, BTC, USDC, ETH  and other stablecoins have anchored most of that growth. But these assets have also laid the foundation for what's coming next, by getting institutions comfortable with onchain infrastructure…

The onchain collateral supernova

…Now, Wall Street is racing to tokenize treasuries, funds, credit, and equities. “Crypto native” collateral will keep growing, but the tokenization wave has the potential to be orders of magnitude larger.

Onchain credit markets will accelerate tokenization growth because they make tokenized assets more productive: they becomes programmable collateral that people can borrow against 24/7, in seconds.

In the not so distant future, we’ll have tens of thousands of tokenized assets and $ trillions more in value onchain. Humans and agents will flock to the fastest and most composable system.

In credit, Morpho is poised to be that system.

First orders of business

It’s day one for me, but it’s already clear a lot of my work will rhyme with what I focused on over the last 7+ years scaling Coinbase’s institutional and infrastructure businesses: helping make our partners successful.

Over the next few weeks, I’ll be on a listening tour. If you’re working on credit products - as a fintech, lender, curator, asset issuer or something else - drop me a line. We want to hear from you and help you grow.

Last but not least: we’re hiring! …Across GTM and beyond. Come get in touch if you’re as excited about the Morpho vision as I am.

Let’s go.

text:
Thinking out loud. I think I can see the "ai bitcoin" or "ai money" thing now. 

(Envelope math not real numbers...)

As I've explained $PRL lets you go from selling $1.00 of inference per hour of GPU time to now getting $0.99 inference revenue (efficiency loss) and then having $0.15 of PRL. 

So your revenue goes up 14% to $1.14 for that hour of GPU. 

Game theory says eventually the inference gets sold for less money as inference providers use the subsidy to compete for more customers (sell PRL in market).

Buyers, as I've noted, buy PRL for it's potential energetic hard money properties.

But what's more interesting is that the value of the inference in a way accrues to the PRL too. 

Because at equilibrium the inference provider will have PRL on their balance sheet, so they need to get a sense of the value of electricity, PRL, GPU depreciation, and how it all fits together in their business.

I believe if these ratios stabilize (such as in my example of 14% revenue to PRL, and a share of inference costs discounted to PRL etc) then PRL will be something the accountants need to model just like any other balance sheet asset.

Early accounting will bias towards dumping it all immediately. If price is good over time, that will change to strategic holding based on expected price appreciation.

Now, feed that strategic holding through the rest of the accounting team spreadsheet with all the inputs to inference (GPU, electric, model intelligence). 

The ratios will be well understood by accounting and finance teams. The value of PRL on balance sheet today will be connected to the value of future inference (and intelligence).

I can at least wave my hands a little more clearly at "pearl is ai money" or "pearl is ai bitcoin" language. 

Needs to be cleared up but I think it works. 

Sorry if this sounds insane.

text:
David Silver is one of the all-time greats. He was the creator of AlphaGo, which changed the course of history by showing that neural nets could achieve superhuman performance for the first time.

He also has a unique intuition and knack for forecasting when things will happen in AI. With computer Go, he predicted the Lee Sodol outcome 10 years before, right to the year. He got the year right for Starcraft and won a bet inside Deepmind. Same for AlphaProof. Same for the IMO.

David's prediction for superintelligence: 3 years. !!! He has a strong sense that now is the time to build a superleaner, and that superlearners are now possible, thanks to the enormous progress in compute, simulators, autoresearch, and the sophistication of technology in the stack since the AlphaGo days.

What is a “super learner”? A super learner discovers all knowledge from its own experience. Start from nothing (no internet pre-training), and go beyond human knowledge. Drop it into any stream of experience, simulated or physical, and the superlearner learns.

He expects the progress will be rapid. When you get the recipe for a superlearner just right and remove humans from the development loop altogether, a superlearner can learn extremely quickly. Just look at AlphaGo. AlphaGo took two years to develop with humans in the loop. When David and his team at @GoogleDeepMind got the formula for AlphaZero correctly, it surpassed the human-developed algorithms in just a few hours. Human data is a shortcut, but you have to let go of the human data to shoot beyond it.

In January, David left GDM to found @IneffableLabs, a research-led lab with one mission: build a "super learner" that discovers all knowledge from its own experience, and make first contact with superintelligence. 

He joins us with co-founder Lasse Espeholt, who built IMPALA and SEED RL, the foundations of scaled-up RL, and now runs Ineffable's compute.

A few things we cover in this conversation. 

 — What a super learner is: depth (start from nothing, go beyond human knowledge) and breadth (drop it into any stream of experience, simulated or physical). The human brain is the only existence proof

 — Why they're giving up human data: AlphaGo took two years with humans in the loop. AlphaZero outperformed it in a few hours. "You have to let go of the human data to shoot past the competition"

 — Crucibles: simulated worlds with enough emergent complexity (physics engines, millions of interacting agents) for an agent to rediscover technology, science, maths and language on its own

— Simple rewards, emergent complexity: evolution optimized fitness and got all of life. Don't breadcrumb the objective, give the agent something simple to optimize in a world with a lot to learn about

 — Go as the existence proof: one agent is the most boring game imaginable, two agents is "an infinite onion of layers of complexity"

 — Why human language is probably not the endpoint for reasoning, and how training on it bakes in a flat earth and the four humors

 — Can superintelligence be built in simulation? If the sim is Turing complete, computation, economics, language and maths are all expressible, and it happens 10-100x faster and safer

 — Alignment: language-based monitoring is reaching its limits as agents learn to say one thing and do another. Shadow actions, superintelligences monitoring superintelligences, and building a real science of how they interact peacefully

 — Accelerate in simulation, pace in the real world: Ineffable will gate real-world deployment on evidence that it goes well

 — Timing as the determinant: Silver called Computer Go to the year, then StarCraft, then the IMO. He thinks this is the moment
 
 — Predictions: True superintelligence within three years.

Timestamps:
 0:00 – Introduction
 1:09 – What held true from Go to today, and what the LLM era changed
 3:35 – Why leave DeepMind to start a new lab
 5:58 – Why "Ineffable" (and the secret second reason)
 7:03 – Lasse's path: scaling RL at DeepMind and Google Brain
 9:31 – Defining a super learner and first contact
 12:35 – Super learners vs. LLMs that make discoveries
 13:59 – Day to day: the RL stack, crucibles and human-journey milestones
 16:13 – Don't breadcrumb the objective: simple rewards, emergent complexity
 21:16 – What a crucible looks like
 24:14 – Go: one agent is boring, two is infinite
 25:41 – Will agents rediscover language?
 27:22 – Removing human priors: AlphaGo to AlphaZero
 32:05 – Keeping human bias out of the crucibles
 33:35 – Confidence, timing and super forecasting
 36:24 – Is compute the driver?
 38:13 – The ceiling on simulation and Rich Sutton's objection
 43:44 – Alignment and the science of superintelligence
 47:45 – Monitoring agents that don't think in English
 51:01 – Pacing the frontier
 52:54 – The compute setup: Vera Rubin on GCP
 55:18 – Training, inference, simulation and RL scaling laws
 57:40 – IMPALA and SEED RL
 1:00:58 – 20 people and the compute-per-person ratio
 1:04:49 – A research-led culture
 1:05:47 – Predictions

text:
“They can't trace Monero, bullshit.” Let's be clear:

Zcash leaks at its own edge. When coins go into or out of the shielded pool, the amount shows on Zcash’s own chain. Monero has no edge like that. Every amount is hidden (RingCT), every receiver gets a one-time address, and every spend sits among decoys. You can’t follow coins across Monero’s ledger.

But a thief doesn’t live inside Monero. They have to get in and get out, and the doors are often public.

A hypothetical scenario, using XMR1 on Hyperliquid:

- The thief swaps stolen USDC into XMR1. Hyperliquid is a public chain, so the wallet, size and time are all on the record.
- They withdraw to native XMR through the bridge in 9 lots of ~210, one about every 40 minutes. The withdrawals are public. Nobody sees what happens inside Monero after that.
- Two days later, 9 deposits of ~209.9 XMR come back through the bridge and mint XMR1 to a fresh wallet. Same count, same sizes less fees, same 40-minute rhythm. Or the same shape turns up somewhere else, as BTC out of a swap desk worth the same at that hour.

All we can do is match the way in to the way out. But that leaves plenty to go on: how many lots, how big, when, and many more markers that people don't realise.

That’s not a weakness in Monero. Monero does its job.

Almost everything leaves a trace. Walk through a room and you leave a scent. You can’t see it, but the right sensor picks it up. On-chain it’s the same: the trail is always there, you just need the right instrument to see it.

Today @dolapo and I are introducing Scuba, the shared context engine for teams and their agents.

text:
(1/7) I'd like to provide some additional context for the remarks that can be found in this interview.

(2/7) My discomfort with the attention being paid to existential risk---and with the ongoing dominance of the public discussion of such risks by a few so-called thought leaders---is that there's an elephant in the room that is being missed.  That elephant is the effect of all of this discussion on young people, and indeed the effect---beginning with social media a decade ago---of information technology on young lives broadly speaking.

(3/7) I recently read an interview by Jill Lepore in which she reports on discussions that she had recently with a group of college students: "They had just three things to say. One, social media completely destroyed their childhoods.  Two, AI is destroying their college education and their likely prospects for employment. And three, what the hell are we all doing?"  To add a fourth bullet that I've heard in similar discussions: "I'm not going to have children, because the existential risk is just too high."

(4/7) Please contemplate such a statement, those of you who think that it's OK that the public, widely diffused, discussion coming from seemingly authoritative figures is so adamant about existential risk.

(5/7) Let me add that I have little interest in a debate about what "superintelligence" might mean, or whether we're currently seeing the emergence of superintelligence.  For what it's worth, I would certainly agree that the solution of extremely challenging math problems (for example) exhibits a very impressive form of intelligence, although I would want to argue that such intelligence is impossible to dissociate from the collective of humans that provided data to the machine learning system (which itself has become a kind of collective).

(6/7) Such philosophical debates are entertaining and even important, but when they then head in the direction of "when such superintelligence emerges, there's a good chance that it will want to kill all humans", I say "science fiction".  Again, I don't think that it's bad to consider such thoughts, but I strongly believe that it's bad for society, and especially young people, for such thoughts, unaccompanied by any serious real-world analysis, to become a dominant form of discourse of the era.
(7/7) We are damaging human lives, and the consequences of that damage will no doubt be a major theme of the next several decades.

text:
摩根士丹利提醒投资者：SpaceX增长潜力最大的一块业务，可能还没被你放进估值里。马斯克随后回复：“没错，这是件非常大的事。”

Adam Jonas说的，是“分布式推理云”。名字有点绕，先翻成白话：AI训练完成后，每次回答问题、识别路况、指挥机器人，都要继续消耗算力，这叫推理。而未来需要AI的设备，会散落在道路、工厂、港口，甚至没有稳定网络的地方。

这就带来一个问题：机器人越来越多，难道每一个都要装下最强模型、配齐最贵的芯片？一种可能的架构，是设备在本地完成必须立即处理的动作，再通过网络调用其他算力、共享信息。Jonas押注的是：随着这些实体AI越来越密集，它们协同工作时，整个网络能完成的任务也会增加。

SpaceX的想象空间就从这里打开了。星链已经在做连接，而Jonas看的是这张连接网络，未来能怎样参与AI的运行。今天客户付钱买的是联网；如果以后机器人还需要持续调用推理、交换信息，连接背后就可能长出新的服务收入。这是对未来商业模式的推演，还要看实际产品、时延、成本和收费方式怎样落地。

所以我会特别关注他那句提醒：未来一年，投资者会越来越多地听到“分布式推理云”和“实体AI集群”。他是在告诉市场，研究SpaceX时，别只数卫星、用户和发射次数，还得开始问：这张网络最终会连接多少台需要持续思考和协作的机器？

马斯克认可了这个方向，但具体架构和收入兑现仍要往下看。下一步值得盯的，是谁先接入、能完成什么任务，以及愿意为什么付钱。星链每多连接一台机器人，究竟只是多卖一份流量，还是多了一位持续购买AI服务的客户？这两笔生意，估值会差很多。

text:
Quick thoughts on the events I missed over the past two months:

- The XRP bug is a great finding, but the reward was low. But even Ethereum had a $250k max bounty a few months ago, so I wouldn’t criticize Ripple too hard.

- The max cap wasn’t specified in the XRP bounty program, so most hunters didn’t even bother checking it.

- The $50k Vercel bounty is too low. They advertised a $1 million bounty, which is misleading, since there's a $50k max cap. Are they expecting 20 Criticals?

- Other projects continue lowering their bounties or closing programs while hacks increase. I understand that it hurts to pay so many reports, but there’s no coming back from a hack.

- The “Duplicates” problem hasn’t been solved. You can still report a Critical issue, prevent major damage to a project and its users, and they will still try to find a way to pay you nothing while pointing to some non-impactful report as sharing the same root cause. Platforms should address this scam immediately.

- The LLM decompilation movement is pretty cool. It's the end of the era of closed-source code.

- People building security tools that depend on LLM tokens should try to make a profit today, or have a clear plan to sell their company before models get better. There's no long-term plan.

- LLM spam continues to be the main trend for getting bounty rewards. It feels like buying lottery tickets. The more tokens people spend, the more chances they have of landing an actual exploit. Having a unique approach seems to help too. But nobody is performing much better than the model they use, since there's no clear outstanding winner in the leaderboards.

- We’re getting to the end of 2026, and bounty rewards paid haven’t increased 10x with AI. According to Grok, for the top 100 on Immunefi the total earnings were:
* 2026 $16M, 1364 reports
* 2025 $11M, 820 reports
* 2024 $21M, 775 reports 
* 2023 $17M , 559 reports
* 2022 $57M, 443 reports

- What happened with Ledger is worrisome. Keep improving your OpSec, whitehats.

Personal thoughts:

We keep seeing more and more bugs in all kind of software. That's not because of superhuman AI capabilities. It's because how bad we've been building software over decades in terms of security.

Nobody cared about exploits because they were difficult for the average hackers. Now everyone has a low-level-IQ tool that can crack neglected code, and we see the results.

We're in a transition phase, where LLMs trained with human bugs are outperforming the average guys. We'll probably get to an era of LLMs-code-first, with LLM bugs that with unprecedented vulnerabilities.

Yes, LLMs are just that bad at coding, and the current models might not be able to see some obvious errors, since they also have "cognition bias".

I see a bright future for bounty hunters, full of vulnerabilities waiting to be found and prevented. We just need to solve the bug-pocalypse first if we don’t want blackhats to win.

text:
AI机房的债券正在被砸，马斯克却补了一句话：连SpaceX这样的工程团队，都觉得把这些东西建起来非常难。

ZeroHedge今天发帖称，CoreWeave无担保债券相对美国国债的利差首次触及1000个基点，也就是额外要付约10个百分点的风险溢价。它还形容Oracle的相关债券交易表现像深度垃圾债，连Meta的Project Beignet项目债利差也在逼近纪录高位。注意，这是债市在提高风险要价，不能直接理解成这些公司已经违约，或者信用评级都变成了垃圾级。

马斯克随后回应：超级计算数据中心的需求确实很旺，但拿到钱，和真正建成拥有巨大供电、散热、网络能力的复杂系统，是两件不同的事。他甚至搬出SpaceX的工程能力来作比较，然后承认：“连我们都觉得非常难。”

这句话放到融资里，就很容易理解了。签下客户、借到钱、买到GPU之后，还得把电接进来，让散热和网络跑起来，最后按约交付。假设上线晚了半年，客户收入可能跟着推迟，债务利息却未必陪你一起等。项目纸面上越赚钱，大家越容易忽略中间这段最烧钱、也最容易出问题的时间。

债市正在追问一个股票市场容易跳过去的问题：你说未来算力需求巨大，我相信；但你的机房什么时候能开始收钱，收的钱够不够覆盖建设成本和债务？

这也给“AI需求旺盛，基础设施就都能赢”补上了条件。接下来我会更看重实际通电、交付进度、利用率和现金回款。客户排队等算力，和债主排队收利息，可以同时发生。机房晚一天上线，银行不会因此晚一天计息。

text:
OpenAI 沙特员工在公司执行会议室植入录音设备后被捕

2026年10月13日，美国司法部（DOJ）与加州北区联邦检察官办公室解封了一份引发硅谷震动的刑事起诉书：现年35岁的沙特阿拉伯籍OpenAI产品团队工程主管阿卜杜勒拉赫曼·阿尔福赞（Abdulrahman Alfozan），因涉嫌在OpenAI旧金山总部的高管会议室秘密安装窃听设备，已被联邦调查局（FBI）正式逮捕并收押。在加入OpenAI之前，阿尔福赞曾担任Meta高级系统工程师及初创公司Nash的创始工程师，于2025年7月入职OpenAI。

根据法庭文件披露，这起看似具备电影质感的商业间谍案，在执行层面上却充满了令人啼笑皆非的细节。9月28日前后，阿尔福赞潜入平时专门用于讨论核心机密研究、产品路线图、商业战略及政府合作的高管会议室，将一个加密录音设备插在电视机背面的USB接口上，并用一团卫生纸进行伪装。9月30日，该装置被OpenAI员工意外发现。10月5日，不知情的阿尔福赞再次潜入会议室查看电视机背面，甚至在当天将一个装有自己钱包、身份证件以及另一个同款录音设备的背包遗落在了办公区，被安保人员当场截获。

然而，本案最极具赛博朋克黑色幽默的一幕在于破案过程：OpenAI在官方声明中确认，公司安全团队直接调用了自家的AI大模型来拆解该硬件设备、分析底层线索并锁定内鬼。调查人员顺藤摸瓜地发现，阿尔福赞不仅在公司内部办公软件中频繁检索高管日程与会议室位置，还在9月24日至30日期间，借用其配偶关联的聊天机器人（Chatbot）账号，向AI提问“如何制作并隐藏连续录音设备”、“如何添加Wi-Fi远程监听”、“如何加密存储卡”，甚至直接把涉案设备独有的网络标识符（MAC/SSID信息）喂给了AI进行故障排查。10月9日，阿尔福赞被解雇并遭FBI逮捕，目前面临非法截获口头通信的联邦指控，最高可判处5年监禁及25万美元罚款。

---- 下面是让 Gemini 4 Argon 写的故事版 ----

【故事版】《卫生纸里的幽灵，与出卖主人的神明》

一、 深夜的提问者

九月下旬的旧金山，深夜的冷雾漫过米申区（Mission District）的街道。

35岁的阿卜杜勒拉赫曼·阿尔福赞坐在家中的电脑前，屏幕的幽光映照着他略显紧绷的脸。作为履历光鲜的硅谷精英——前Meta高级系统工程师、如今的OpenAI工程主管——他本该是这座科技圣殿里的核心筑造者之一。但此刻，他的脑海里装的不是下一代大模型的架构，而是总部大楼里那间他无权踏足的“高管会议室”。

那里是权力的中枢。每天，关于未公开的推理模型、数千亿美元的商业盟约、乃至与五角大楼和各国政府的秘密会晤，都在那四面隔音玻璃墙内激荡。

他需要一只“耳朵”。

作为一个习惯了向人工智能寻求一切答案的工程师，阿尔福赞鬼使神差地打开了对话窗口。为了掩人耳目，他特意切换到了妻子名下的账号——但他忘了，底层的设备指纹与网络标识符，早已像影子一样将两个账号死死绑在了一起。

他在键盘上敲下一行行指令：

“如何组装一个能够连续工作的微型音频录制设备？”“怎样为它加上Wi-Fi模块，实现远程监听？”“如何对内存卡进行高强度加密，防止被拆解读取？”

屏幕那头的AI温和、博学、毫无戒心地给出了完美的工程方案。9月27日深夜，当他在调试硬件遇到网络瓶颈时，甚至直接把这台定制窃听器独一无二的网络标识符复制进了对话框。

他以为自己是在向一个没有灵魂的工具请教。他不知道，自己正在向未来的“证人”口述一整份犯罪自白书。

二、 电视机后的“白色伪装”

9月28日，周一。

在此前的几天里，阿尔福赞已经通过公司的生产力工具，像猎犬一样搜遍了办公楼地址、会议室平面图以及高管与外部伙伴的会议日历。走廊尽头的闭路电视（CCTV）记录下了他数次在非授权区域徘徊的身影。

终于，他抓住了高管会议室空置的几分钟空隙，闪身而入。

房间里纤尘不染，巨大的显示屏黑着屏幕，像一面深邃的镜子。阿尔福赞心跳如擂鼓，他掏出那个已经刷好加密固件、焊好Wi-Fi模块的微型录音装置，熟练地摸到电视机背面，将其插进了一个隐蔽的USB供电接口里。

指示灯微弱地闪烁了一下。但问题来了——如果有人恰好歪头看向电视机后方，这个突兀的电子元件依然可能暴露。

受过顶尖计算机工程训练的大脑在这一刻突然短路，回归到了最原始的慌乱。他四下张望，最终从口袋里掏出一团白色的卫生纸，小心翼翼地将这个高科技窃听器裹了起来，塞进电视机背板的阴影里。

在估值数千亿美元、代表着人类最高智慧结晶的AI帝国心脏地带，一团皱巴巴的卫生纸，成了这场跨国商业间谍疑云的滑稽外衣。

三、 算力深处的反猎杀

这团卫生纸的寿命只有48小时。

9月30日，一名OpenAI工作人员在整理高管会议室时，注意到了电视机后面那团不合时宜的白色异物。剥开卫生纸，一枚精致而复杂的改装录音设备露了出来。

警报在瞬间拉响，但属于科技巨头的方式是静默无声的。

安保与安全团队封锁了消息。放在过去，排查这样一个加密硬件的来源需要耗费数周的法医级电子取证；但在OpenAI，安全专家们做了一个极其符合公司气质的决定——让AI去抓那个背叛AI的人。

安全团队将这枚窃听器的电路特征、加密逻辑、硬件参数以及散发的微弱网络特征码输入到了内部大模型中。算力在硅片间狂飙，模型迅速理解了这台设备的构造与来龙去脉。紧接着，内部日志检索与监控交叉比对全面展开：

谁没有权限，却屡次出现在高管会议室门前的摄像头里？

谁在内部办公工具里疯狂检索领导层的会议日程与房间号？

更致命的是——当系统比对那枚设备独有的网络标识符时，一段发生于9月27日至28日的聊天记录直接浮出了水面。

真相揭晓得如此之快，甚至带着一丝荒谬的宿命感：那个小偷在作案前，竟然亲自用自家关联的系统，手把手教自己怎么作案。

OpenAI没有打草惊蛇，而是 quietly（悄然地）拨通了FBI的电话，并留下了一张张开的大网。

四、 消失的猎物与遗落的背包

10月5日，距离设备被拔除已经过去了五天。

这五天里，阿尔福赞备受煎熬。他原本期待着远程Wi-Fi能传回源源不断的音频流，但接收端却是一片死寂。是电视机断电了？还是加密脚本崩溃了？

他决定冒险回去看一眼。

监控镜头冷冷地注视着一切：阿尔福赞再次溜进了那间高管会议室，径直走到电视机旁，探头往屏幕背后望去。

空的。那团卫生纸，连同他精心改装的设备，消失得无影无踪。

一股寒意从脚底直冲头顶。他意识到事情败露了。极度的恐慌瞬间击碎了他的理智，他在匆忙撤离办公区时，甚至犯下了一个比“卫生纸伪装”还要致命的低级错误——他把随身的背包落在了公司里。

几分钟后，巡逻的安保人员发现了这个无人看管的背包。拉开拉链，里面静静地躺着阿尔福赞的钱包、身份证件，以及第二个一模一样的改装录音设备。

人证、物证、监控轨迹、搜索记录、AI对话日志，在这一刻形成了完美得近乎教科书般的证据闭环。

五、 尾声

2026年10月9日，周五。OpenAI向阿尔福赞下达了终止雇佣关系的通知；几乎在同一时刻，早已等候多时的FBI特工亮出了手铐。

10月13日，身穿囚服的阿尔福赞首次在旧金山联邦法院出庭。好消息是，OpenAI确认核心的模型权重、源代码和客户数据均未被染指；坏消息是，这位昔日的硅谷高管将面临最高五年的铁窗生涯。

在这场短短十余天的暗战里，最令人玩味的或许不是卫生纸包裹的U盘，也不是装满罪证的遗落背包，而是那个静静运行在服务器里的AI模型。在9月27日的深夜，它曾毫无保留地解答了人类关于“如何隐秘窃听”的请教；而在三天后的清晨，当安全人员将证物摆在它面前时，它也同样毫无保留地，指认出了那个在黑夜里向它提问的人。

text:
1) Trying again.
 TLDR: Everyone can win. Open-source, frontier labs, infrastructure, applications and most importantly the American people.
 
I understand all of the jitters about Anthropic losing share, real rates, spreads and second derivatives. Still think the most likely future outcome is a hybrid, multi-model future where almost everyone wins, open-weight tokens are likely the overwhelming majority of tokens, the dominant frontier model companies still do well albeit perhaps not the outcome that seemed possible in May and AI infrastructure/applications benefit immensely from the increased fragmentation, competition and lower margins at the model layer.
 
Lower margins at the model layer mechanically drive higher compute demand as long as someone is willing to pay for the training. And Jensen is obviously willing to be the “trainer of last resort.” As below-market compute contracts signed in 24/25 roll-off and reprice higher, cloud and neocloud revenue should continue to accelerate which will help address financing fears; I think we may be near peak external financing for this buildout. Noteworthy that using data from 3Fourteen Research, B200 clusters will generate a 37% IRR *if* their rental price declines 40% per year. Prices are still going up, but that IRR math is too ridiculous to print. 37% IRRs available at scale should get funded.

Re: this weekends controversy about MOUs, Anthropic’s $413 billion of real contractual commitments sounds scary. Reality is that it works out to roughly $31 billion of annual cloud spend, which is easily internally financed given their reported ARR, and $161 billion of spend at Broadcom which will be financed by Broadcom and private credit.

Continue to believe fragmentation at the model layer is the best outcome for ordinary Americans and humans everywhere. As I have said before, do not trust any 5-20 individuals to make the best possible decisions about the direction of this technology. I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that they encompass the diversity of human values across the world and richness of human variation. And I want an AI that shares my own personal values. Safety, freedom and the maximization of human agency through democratization, distribution and diffusion vs. centralization. History has spoken on the dangers of the latter path.

Finally, from my perspective anything that slows this buildout down is net positive over the long-term as the biggest risk and worst outcome is an *actual* overbuild. We are structurally short watts, wafers and increasingly capital. That is all good. God forbid we were still in ZIRP, TSM ramped capex to 3x their current plan and we weren’t short turbine blades: there would almost certainly be an overbuild and a bubble. That would be terrible. Slower and smoother for longer is better both for investors and for the world. A terrible cyber event is the most plausible near term bear case IMHO, but AI cyberdefense ramping quickly and I was happy to hear Sholto say that cyber probably becomes defense dominant in the near future.

10 OpSec rules every crypto holder MUST follow ↓

8. Secure your home – Install alarms, cameras, and reinforced locks

text:
从Mark Minervini的书 Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard 提炼的14条核心 Mindset

以下为依据原书思想的归纳与应用延伸，非作者逐字引文。

1.我可以认真捍卫自己的交易纪律，同时随时修正自己的市场判断。

把判断与自尊绑定，容易让卖出变成“承认自己不够聪明”。判断可以修正，风险边界需要坚守。保护资本，无须等待自己完全想通或承认看错。

2.我可以放弃最低的价格，等待更充分的强势证据。

等待趋势和买点成熟，往往需要支付更高价格。我愿意为确认付费，同时要求入场位置仍有合理的风险收益比。上涨本身无法代替买点判断。

3.我可以喜欢便宜的东西，同时警惕股票带给我的“便宜感”。

价格下降、估值降低、风险收益比改善，是三个不同的判断。过去更贵，无法证明现在值得买。每次买入，都需要重新检验增长、预期和风险。

4.我可以长期看好一家公司，同时承认这次买入的时机或仓位规模有问题。

公司前景、买入时机、仓位大小，需要分别判断。退出一笔交易，无须先证明公司的长期故事已经失败。长期看好，也需要与当前风险相匹配。

5.我可以耐心等待买点，因为好的买点能让我更清楚地识别错误。

好的买点，同时提供机会和验证条件。买入前，应明确预期行为与失效条件。入场依据越模糊，持有后越容易依赖故事解释一切。

6.我可以接受小额失败，同时认真保护继续参与市场的能力。

重大亏损会同时消耗资本、恢复时间和行动信心。**我允许合理的试错成本，同时防止一次错误长期限制自己的选择。**止损应在买入前就被心理接受。

7.我可以有很多亏损交易，同时仍然建立有效的盈利体系。

长期结果由胜率、平均盈利、平均亏损和交易成本共同决定。**我用一组可比较的交易评价方法，用具体规则评价单笔执行。**避免为减少失败次数而拖延止损。

8.我可以逐步增加风险，但需要让实际反馈支持这个决定。

加仓需要新的依据，亏损本身不会赋予加仓资格。仓位应随有效证据增加，随不利反馈重新评估。尤其警惕为了降低成本，临时把失败的趋势交易改成左侧布局。

9.我可以暂时解释不了价格变化，同时先尊重已经出现的风险证据。

价格行为可能先于财报恶化。我无需解释清楚所有变化，才开始管理风险。如果任何走势都能支持同一个结论，就需要检查自己的判断是否还能被证伪。

10.我可以对机会保持耐心，同时对失效条件保持敏感。

等待机会、容忍正常整理，都需要耐心；触及退出条件后继续拖延，则需要警惕。给予交易的时间，应与它持续满足的条件相匹配。

11.我可以选择自己的交易风格，同时接受这种选择必然带来的遗憾。

短线交易可能卖早，长期持有可能回吐阶段利润。选择一种收益路径，也要接受它的代价。避免每天用另一种策略的最佳结果，否定自己的决定。

12.我可以接受卖出后的遗憾，也可以在新的条件成立时重新买入。

原书允许股票重新形成合格买点后再次入场。关键是独立评估新交易：如果我从未持有、也从未卖出，现在还会以同样的依据，买入同样的数量吗？

13.我可以不知道市场接下来怎么走，同时提前知道自己如何响应。

提前想清止损、盈利保护、重新入场和意外情况，能减少临场情绪干扰。交易信心可以来自准备充分，无须依赖对未来接近百分之百的确定感。

14.我可以坚持练习，同时不把重复错误当成经验积累。

重复既能强化纪律，也能强化坏习惯。守纪律的亏损可以是合理试错，违规后的盈利仍需要纠正。复盘要把经验转化为下一次具体、可检验的行动。

text:
Grok Bot does my food shopping in less than 3 minutes. 

Doing it myself would probably take an hour at the shops or 30 minutes ordering online.

 How do I do this? I have a Grok Bot food prep team:

1 - A Meal Organiser that knows the lunches and dinners I like.

2 - A Shopper that fills my grocery cart.

3 - A Cooking Bot that walks me through preparing the meals.

I tell my Chief of Staff how many days I need. The team handles the planning and cart, and I check out myself.

When it’s time to cook, I ask for the instructions. My meals take less than 20 minutes.

Here’s the prompt to set up your own food prep team. 

Start of prompt-------

“Set up a food prep team for me: three specialist Bots reporting to you, my Chief of Staff.

Start by asking me for any missing details in my food profile. Show me the proposed Bot descriptions before creating them.

MY FOOD PROFILE

Diet: [my diet or dietary goals].
Servings: [how many people each meal should feed].
Never include: [allergies, intolerances and disliked foods].
Preferences: [cooking time, budget and ingredient preferences].
Grocery store: [Add store link].
Meal bank: [6–10 meals I like, or ask me and suggest some].

Save my confirmed profile for future use.

1 - MEAL ORGANISER
When I tell you how many days and which meals, build a plan from my meal bank.

Follow my food profile. Ask about ingredients I already have so we can avoid buying them again.

Return the meal plan and one combined shopping list with quantities matched to the number of servings. Include any extras I request.

Wait for my approval before handing the list to the Shopper.

2 - SHOPPER

After I approve the plan, open my grocery store’s website and fill the cart with the approved shopping list.

Pick sensible pack sizes. Check the existing cart before adding items to avoid duplicates.

For out-of-stock items, choose the closest suitable match within my food profile. Flag anything uncertain rather than guessing, especially where an allergy or dietary restriction is involved.

Stop before checkout. Never choose a delivery slot, place the order or pay.

Return the cart total, substitutions and anything you couldn’t find. I will review the cart and check out myself.

3 - COOKING

When I name a meal from the plan, give me simple cooking instructions using the ingredients we selected, including any approved substitutions.

Include preparation time, cooking time, quantities and steps in order. Explain when to start each component so everything finishes together.

Keep the recipe within my agreed cooking-time preference. Flag any extra preparation needed in advance.

HOW WE WORK TOGETHER

I tell you:

‘Plan 3 days of lunch and dinner, plus these extras: [items].’

You get the Meal Organiser to draft the plan and show it to me.

After my approval, send the shopping list to the Shopper.

Report back when the cart is ready, including anything that needs my attention.

When I ask what to cook, use the current plan and get the Cooking Bot to guide me.

For the initial grocery-store connection, open the website and let me complete the login myself.

Confirm which Bots are created and whether the store is accessible. Tell me if any setup step remains incomplete.”

End of prompt-------

The biggest saving is having fewer everyday decisions to make, then having a team carry them through.

text:
The first AI Assistant Consumer Travel Report is live!

We spent the past week testing travel capabilities across 5 AI assistants: Instinct, Muse, GrokBot, Dots & Miso

🥇 Miso - fastest & most capable, omitted budget flights
🥈 Instinct - very fast but couldn't do rescheduling
🥉 GrokBot - medium speed, fully capable, very verbose
💐 Dots - very very slow but fully capable
💐 Muse - fairly capable, fairly slow, very verbose

Each assistant was tested across the following dimensions:
1. Booking time
2. Onboarding flow
3. Booking execution
4. Seat selection
5. Travel profile
6. Cancellation
7. Rebooking
8. Proactiveness

The report outlines some unique findings:

> There are three different booking methods used across the board: browser use, API access & OTA

> Miso was the fastest, at ~3 min to book where as Dots was the slowest, at ~33 min to book

> All 5 succeeded in booking a flight, but Muse wasn't able to change/upgrade a seat

> Instinct & Muse were not able to change the flight as the API provider they use, Duffel, doesn't give them that functionality

> Everyone biased towards cheaper options except Miso, who wasn't able to book basic economy flights

> Miso was the only one to ask for traveler details, loyalty number, and known travel number unprompted

Want new dimensions tested for the next report?

Let me know!

Elon Musk is worth $908 billion, and this weekend he asked world-class engineers to come join Tesla. Tesla once tried to cancel the sale of one car to the man who named the company. Martin Eberhard had already paid for Founders Series car number 2, and he had to sue to get it.

Eberhard started Tesla with Marc Tarpenning in 2003 and was its first CEO. Musk wrote the biggest check of the first round, became chairman and later blamed Eberhard for the Roadster's delays and overruns.

Ledger theft, day two. Since yesterday the thief has pushed ether through Tornado Cash three times, and each time on into Zcash's shielded pool. We followed every lot out the far side. Here is how, step by step.

1. THE SAME BUILD, THREE TIMES
An ether wallet pays a fresh splitter. The splitter pays four fresh wallets. The four drop it into Tornado Cash's 100, 10 and 1 ETH pools. Minutes, every time.

Run 1, yesterday 15:17: 1,254 ETH. Run 2, today 09:42: 1,291 ETH. Run 3, today 11:56: 450 ETH from 0xfa4EaBB840A33C156E600311433AE261CBfCb0e2, in the pools by 12:15.

2. OUT OF TORNADO CASH
The mixer breaks the link between a deposit and a withdrawal. We do not need the link. Our tooling fingerprints the withdrawal transactions themselves: how each one is constructed, who constructs it, and when. 

Yesterday's 65 withdrawals (1,084 ETH) and today's 96 (1,726 ETH) all carry the same signature. The six other withdrawals from those pools in today's windows do not. Run 3 came out from 12:18 into 0x0d697aa182801566d87adc86e68e95fd3b2f5f82 (213 ETH) and 0x676b16cc18542f37d202a1a79ac05463395496a4 (122 ETH), and 195 ETH of it was inside a cross-chain swap service by 12:38. Forty-two minutes, end to end.

3. INTO ZCASH, AND OUT AGAIN
The swap service turns the ether into shielded ZEC, where sender, amount and recipient vanish. But the service's own shielding of each lot is public, and from it we derive a value signature for that lot's exit, then scan every transparent exit from the pool. 108 of 108 exits across both days match their lot to the zatoshi. text:
Jev as a judge for LLM evals!

JevEval uses Jev as the judge for custom LLM evals instead of relying on another generative LLM for every evaluation.

The idea is pretty simple.

You define the exact decisions you want the evaluator to make, Jev evaluates each one and returns probabilities, and DeepEval uses those results to calculate the final score.

For example, with an AI agent you can evaluate the trace itself, checking whether the agent selected the right tools, followed the expected sequence of actions, and actually completed the task.

Jev handles those semantic judgments, while the scoring logic stays outside the model.

That is the main difference from a normal LLM-as-a-judge setup.

With a generative judge, the model often has to interpret the rubric, reason about the response, and generate the evaluation itself.

With JevEval, you define the decision structure upfront.

You can also assign different weights to different checks or use `strict_mode` when every requirement needs to pass.

So if one part of the agent workflow matters more than another, you can reflect that directly in the scoring logic instead of leaving the entire evaluation to the judge model.

Key capabilities:

- Evaluate agent outputs and traces with Jev
- Define custom checks as bounded decisions
- Use yes/no, score, and closed-choice questions
- Weight different checks or require all of them to pass
- Evaluate both single-turn outputs and multi-turn conversations

This is where Jev makes a lot of sense for evals.

If you already know what needs to be checked, you can define those decisions upfront, let Jev handle the semantic judgment, and keep the final scoring deterministic.

I’ve shared the DeepEval post in the comments.

Most open RL environments cluster around the same few domains. Almost none are long-context time series.

Prime Intellect RL resident @nzuma0 built one. AnomalyXL is an infinitely scalable synthetic generator with programmatic ground truth, written in verifiers.

He then trained a 4B TimeRLM on it with prime-rl, generating fresh data every step, with the model recursively calling sub-agents via nano-rlm to localize anomalies across 131k datapoints. It transfers zero-shot to ECG, sleep and observability data.
author: PrimeIntellect
quoted_text:
Frontier Time Series Language Models struggle with precise anomaly localization over long contexts, when useful signals might be hidden in hours of recordings.

In our new paper we trained a tiny Recursive Language Model to SoTA performance on long context time series.

We introduce AnomalyXL, an infinitely scalable synthetic time-series generator with programmatic ground truth answers. 

Training our RLM formulation on this RL environment transfers to real world anomaly detection in Software Observability, ECG and Sleep data.

text:
ROBINHOOD CHAIN IS DEAD 

Is the take I keep seeing all over my timeline right now, and I honestly think it’s a stupid one.

Outside of the OGs like Solana, BNB and Ethereum, we haven’t had a new chain break out and capture this much attention since Base, and four months in, Robinhood Chain is already the third-biggest chain by DEX volume over the past month, behind only Solana and Ethereum.

Robinhood Chain’s best week was about four times bigger than anything Base did in its first eight months, back when Base was actually doing well, and it got back above its launch high around five months sooner than Base did.

New chains move a lot like coins do at launch, where the early attention sends them up and then they pull back to retest the level they broke out from. That retest is exactly where Robinhood Chain’s volume is sitting right now, and it’s the same level Base’s biggest run started from.

Trading has slowed down since September, but TVL has kept climbing and just hit a new all-time high this week, which means the capital is sticking around even though the hype has cooled off a bit.

If you’re lumping Robinhood Chain in with every other new L2, you’re missing the biggest thing it has going for it, which is a stock brokerage with close to 29 million users, and less than 1% of them are onchain on any given day. With free swaps running until the end of the year and 24/7 stock token trading on the way, that’s a lot of runway for a chain that’s only four months old.

CT is an echo chamber. Once takes like “it’s dead” and “Base 2.0” get a bit of engagement, you start seeing them everywhere, to the point where they feel like the consensus, but the data doesn’t support that narrative.

Ultimately it comes down to what Vlad and the team do from here. He just did an AMA going over his plans for the chain and asking people what they want to see, and there’s talk of a lot more support coming from Robinhood. This is a company that built one of the biggest retail brokerages in the US, and I can’t see them settling for less in crypto.

Today’s selloff just makes the worries look overdone in the semi/AI space. The market is nervous about three things right now and I don't think any of them hold up in the next couple of weeks;

1) CXMT. China's memory champion is the fear of the week. But its push into the next generation of DRAM architecture looks more like a 2030 story than a near term one and without access to EUV lithography it will face a significant cost and yield disadvantage.

2) $AVGO’s comments in Singapore. I think the market misread these. My read is that Hock Tan was describing memory shortages easing, not memory heading into oversupply. Those are very different things.

3) AI capital and power. These are real constraints over the long run. But everything coming out of SemiconWest this week points the other way: the industry is short compute, and equipment makers are being asked to speed up tool deliveries and add meaningful capacity for 2028–2030.

text:
HIP-5 is a debate about what Hyperliquid’s success should be worth.

The proposal would redirect an initial 1% of protocol fees, potentially rising to 5%, into a second Assistance Fund that buys ecosystem tokens selected through HYPE staker voting.

The idea is simple: use Hyperliquid’s revenue to support the projects building around it, not just to buy back HYPE. 

But there’s a trade-off.

If a project needs protocol-funded buying to sustain demand for its token, is that real ecosystem growth or just subsidised demand?

And if the ecosystem grows, does that value actually flow back to HYPE holders?

Hyperliquid already has a powerful value-accrual mechanism. Its existing Assistance Fund uses protocol fees to buy HYPE from the open market. HIP-5 introduces a different idea: some of that economic power could be used to help other tokens grow.

Supporters see a way to attract builders and strengthen the ecosystem. Critics see a potential dilution of HYPE’s value-capture thesis.

The real test is whether buying ecosystem tokens creates lasting economic activity, or simply creates buyers that wouldn’t otherwise exist.

Because a stronger ecosystem and a stronger HYPE token can reinforce each other, but they aren’t automatically the same thing.

HIP-5 remains a proposal, not an approved change. But Hyperliquid soon too 🫵🏼

text:
Legacy media is increasingly hostile to prediction markets, including this misleading poll.

States with out of control spending depend on tax revenue from casinos, which prediction markets threaten.

States become financially dependent on casinos and promote them, like New York State under Kathy Hochul.

So mainstream media enters the fray on behalf of the states and their politicians. It becomes cool among journalists to be against prediction markets.

Yet unlike casinos, prediction markets produce a socially valuable product: predictions.

It's information that anyone can use. Increasingly, private companies, the government, and even the Weather Channel uses the information from prediction markets.

Polling is an art that can distort perceptions. In this poll funded by Reuters, respondents were asked if they supported or opposed "wagering money" in prediction markets, and if they thought this was gambling.

I would imaging that most would be opposed to "wagering money". But that's precisely what makes prediction markets different from casinos.

People who use prediction markets do not "wager money" any more than stock traders do. They buy a contract. Buying a contract is what allows prediction markets to produce a price signal, which allows them to make predictions.

Yes, the underlying motivation -- greed -- produces the outcome. That's what happens in capitalism. People want to make money. They try to make more. Having skin in the game puts a lot of pressure on traders to get things right.

And so the markets end up making reliable predictions. A socially valuable result that anyone can use.

But this isn't blackjack. These are real events, and real, socially valuable information is being produced by traders.

So when you call it "wager money", you provide poll respondents with the frame the presupposes the answer you want to hear.

The survey's wording biased the results.

And it makes prediction markets look less popular than they are. Why would the pollsters do something like that? I've told you my theory. But we don't know for sure.

Now, unlike people blowing money at casinos, successful traders on platforms like Kalshi are much, much better educated than the general population.

These are serious, highly educated people producing socially useful information -- and making money doing it.

Prediction markets do have problems. Insider trading is one. Congress has a huge problem with that.

But interestingly, many Congressmen who are opposed to prediction markets also vote against laws against insider trading in Congress.

They don't like prediction markets, but they don't want to get in trouble for insider trading. Strange.

Another problem is trying to influence events that you are betting on. Say you have power and place a bet in a prediction market. You can use your power to make the bet come true.

This is obviously very bad. So, prediction markets produce unique social value above the casinos they are displacing. But they also have unique risks.

Both are true.

These need to be addressed with good regulation and laws. We need to keep the good, and try to squash the bad.

Fortunately, prediction markets are much better regulated than casinos. They are subjected to more scrutiny and standardization.

But what the above shows is that reducing prediction markets to "wagering money" or "gambling" misses what makes them different and new and exciting.

text:
Yes Chef Group is a food-media company, so it’s only fitting that a random encounter at a restaurant changed everything for its founders.

The story starts when @jacksdiningroom and his co-founder sat next to Sports Illustrated's CEO.

Then they were approached by a group of moms:

“These moms come up to us and are like, ‘My daughters know you.’”

“And [Sports Illustrated's CEO] kind of looked at us. He’s like, ‘Who are you guys and what the hell’s going on?’”

“We’re like, ‘We make content, but we do consulting. This is only 10% of the time. We’ve done 30 million views in two weeks.’”

Then SI's CEO said they were looking to attract a younger audience and do more social-first content.

“So he’s like, ‘What if we did short-form content with you guys?’”

“We kind of just like pitched him the entire world that night.”

“A week later, we got on a call with their whole C-suite team.”

“They offered to match our consulting salaries plus the 50/50 on rev split.”

“Since then, we’ve just never really looked back and we’ve just doubled down on the content.”

text:
Most open RL environments cluster around the same few domains. Almost none are long-context time series.

Prime Intellect RL resident @nzuma0 built one. AnomalyXL is an infinitely scalable synthetic generator with programmatic ground truth, written in verifiers.

He then trained a 4B TimeRLM on it with prime-rl, generating fresh data every step, with the model recursively calling sub-agents via nano-rlm to localize anomalies across 131k datapoints. It transfers zero-shot to ECG, sleep and observability data.
author: vincentweisser
quoted_text:
Frontier Time Series Language Models struggle with precise anomaly localization over long contexts, when useful signals might be hidden in hours of recordings.

In our new paper we trained a tiny Recursive Language Model to SoTA performance on long context time series.

We introduce AnomalyXL, an infinitely scalable synthetic time-series generator with programmatic ground truth answers. 

Training our RLM formulation on this RL environment transfers to real world anomaly detection in Software Observability, ECG and Sleep data.

text:
周一 $META  发了自家第一款前沿模型 Muse Wonder，股价当天涨了3.4%。同一天，卖芯片、卖内存的公司跌成一片，费城半导体指数跌了2.7%。都是 AI 这门生意，有人涨有人跌，市场其实在算一笔账：钱最后落到谁手里。

这次最大的变化是卖法，跑分倒在其次。以前 Meta 的 Llama 是“开放权重”，模型参数直接放出来，谁都能下载到自己机器上跑。Muse 不给下载了。

普通版 Wonder 只能走 Meta 的接口按量付费，每百万 token 输入4美元、输出20美元，token 可以理解成 AI 按字数计费的单位。更强的 Wonder Full 接口里根本没有，只给 Muse Code 的订阅用户。跑分 Meta 说跟 OpenAI、Anthropic 的旗舰差不多，不过这是它自己测的。

Meta 以前把模型白送，现在开始收钱了，市场就愿意给它多算一份收入。芯片公司那头正好反过来：Meta 买芯片的钱，在芯片公司那里是收入，在 Meta 这里是成本，迟早得赚回来。现在国债都有5%，投资人更想知道谁能把这笔成本变成订阅费和接口账单。

但一天的涨跌说明不了什么。已经有开发者在吐槽，跑分最好看的是 Full，接口里能用的却是普通版。最后还得看有没有人真掏钱、一直用下去。

你信得过 Muse 吗？试过的朋友现在还在用吗？拿它干什么，写代码、写东西，还是别的？评论区聊聊。

author: qzhxjhj
quoted_text:
最近一直在参与各种 Launchpad，跟项目方聊得多了以后，我发现大家一开始最关心的，通常都是：

首发资源
控筹
KOL
第一波交易量

但再往后聊更深入，问题就会变成：

第一波热度过去以后，流动性怎么承接？
资产发生变化以后，原来的池子怎么办？
新的用户和需求从哪里继续进来？

很多项目到这一层，路径就开始变得模糊。

所以现在我看一个 Launch，会很在意它有没有把资产后面的生命周期提前策划好。

最近看 @Four_FORM_ 的 4Stock，也是这个角度

股票资产有一个很明显的特点：热点出现得非常快。
一份财报、一条政策、一个 AI 概念，几个小时就可能把一只股票推到市场中心。bStocks 已经给 BNB Chain 带来了一批链上股票资产，但资产覆盖天然存在时间差。
4Stock 补的就是这段窗口。

对于暂时还没有对应 bStock 的热门股票，Four 可以先通过 4Stock 建立对应的链上资产，让 Stock Meme、交易和流动性先跑起来。官方文档里对 4Stock 的定位也很明确：它主要覆盖当前尚未有对应 bStock 的热门美股。

这里有一个细节很重要。

按照 Four文档，4Stock 早期采用申请制：

用户提交 USDC → 平台通过专门管理账户买入对应底层股票 → 再按照实际买入数量 1:1 铸造 4Stock
最终执行价格和到账数量以实际买入为准。

这和 bStocks 的资产支持方式需要分开理解：

bStocks：对应美股由托管方式 1:1 支持
4Stock：https://t.co/pa4OzGBt8g 通过专门管理账户购入底层股票，再按照实际购买数量铸造

更值得关注的是后面⬇️

如果 4Stock 只是解决“先把资产发出来”，价值其实还有限。
比较特别的是，它把后续资产升级和流动性怎么继续往前走也设计进去了。

具体路径是这样的：

Stock Meme 可以先通过 Meme / 4Stock 建立主流动性。
等对应 bStock 就绪以后，官方给出的路径是可以引入 4Stock → 1:1 bStock 的转换（具体仍以届时产品规则和开放状态为准）。

然后是这次我觉得更值得看的 SIH 👇

@PancakeSwap  Infinity 的 Shared Inventory Hook 可以让同一份 Meme 库存同时服务 Meme / 4Stock 和 Meme / bStock 两种配对。

Convert 负责 4Stock → bStock 的资产转换

SIH 负责共享库存和交易过程中的流动性供给
这样原有市场不需要先把主流动性撤掉，再重新建立一套新的池子；随着交易发生，主流动性可以逐步从：

Meme / 4Stock → Meme / bStock

继续往后升级

所以如果让我把这套机制压成一句话：
｜
4Stock 补资产覆盖的时间差，SIH + Convert 补资产升级过程中的流动性断层。

这也是我最近参与 Launchpad 项目后一个很直接的感受：
一个资产最后能不能成为 runner，很多事情其实在Launch 之前就已经决定了一部分：资产怎么承接，流动性怎么延续，用户为什么留下，下一阶段的需求从哪里进来；这些东西如果一开始没有想清楚，前面的热度很容易只剩下一次流量。

所以现在我会拿三个问题去看一个 Launch：

热点来的时候，资产跟得上吗？
资产升级的时候，流动性会不会断？
第一波过去以后，用户凭什么留下？

4Stock 这套机制至少在前两个问题上，给出了一套很清晰的产品思路。

后面我还会继续看几个更实际的问题：

管理账户里的底层股票具体怎么托管和披露
持有人怎么赎回
Convert 真正开放以后深度和滑点表现怎么样

如果 @BNBCHAIN  后面能继续把 资产覆盖速度、流动性连续性、DeFi 可组合性 接起来，我觉得 Stock 这条线会比现在看到的空间更大。
